title: Binary Tree Fundamentals
summary: Core vocabulary and shape/representation of binary trees that every later tree algorithm assumes — height, balance, recursion, and the array-vs-pointer trade-off.

slides.markdown:
A **binary tree** is a node with up to two children, recursively. That single recursive definition is why almost every tree algorithm is naturally written as a recursive function — the base case is an empty (null) subtree, the recursive case processes the current node plus whatever its two subtrees return.

Binary trees anchor roughly half of all DSA interview questions, because they're the simplest structure that captures **hierarchy** — parent/child relationships — which shows up everywhere from file systems to org charts to decision logic. This topic sets the vocabulary and shape questions every later topic in this group assumes you already have.

slides.subTitle: Height, depth, level, and ancestor/descendant
slides.markdown:
A few terms get used precisely and often confused:

- **Depth** of a node — the number of edges from the root down to that node. The root has depth 0.
- **Height** of a node — the number of edges on the longest path from that node down to a leaf. A leaf has height 0.
- **Height of the tree** — the height of the root, i.e., the longest root-to-leaf path.
- **Level** — all nodes at the same depth (level 0 is just the root).
- **Ancestor/descendant** — A is an ancestor of B if A lies on the path from the root to B (and B is then A's descendant). Every node is its own ancestor and descendant by some conventions, so state your convention if it matters.

Depth is measured top-down from the root; height is measured bottom-up from a leaf — mixing them up is the single most common vocabulary slip in tree interviews.

slides.subTitle: Recognizing shape from a picture
slides.markdown:
Four shape classifications that come up constantly and get conflated:

- **Full** — every node has either 0 or 2 children, never exactly 1.
- **Complete** — every level is fully filled except possibly the last, and the last level's nodes are as far left as possible.
- **Perfect** — every internal node has exactly 2 children *and* every leaf is at the same depth (a perfect tree is both full and complete).
- **Degenerate (pathological)** — every node has at most 1 child, so the tree is really a linked list wearing a tree's clothing.

These aren't interchangeable: a complete tree isn't necessarily full (a node could have just a left child), and a full tree isn't necessarily complete (the last level could be filled right-to-left). Perfect is the strict intersection of both.

slides.sectionTitle: Indexing a complete binary tree in an array
slides.markdown:
A **complete** binary tree can be stored in a flat array with no pointers at all: node at index i has children at indices 2i+1 and 2i+2, and a parent at index (i-1)//2. This only works because completeness guarantees no gaps — every array slot up to the tree's size corresponds to a real node.

slides.subTitle: Memory, resizing, and cache behavior
slides.markdown:
| | Array-backed (complete trees only) | Pointer-backed |
|---|---|---|
| Works for any shape | no — requires completeness | yes |
| Memory overhead | none per node | 2+ pointers per node |
| Cache behavior | excellent (contiguous) | poor (scattered) |
| Resizing | needs a full reallocation | none — nodes allocated individually |

Array-backing is the standard implementation for a binary **heap** precisely because a heap is always kept complete by construction — see the `heaps` group. General binary trees (BSTs, arbitrary hierarchies) usually can't guarantee completeness, so they default to pointer-backed nodes despite the worse cache behavior, the same trade-off linked lists make against arrays.

slides.sectionTitle: Why tree algorithms are naturally recursive
slides.subTitle: Base case is null, recursive case is the subtrees
slides.markdown:
A binary tree's own definition is recursive — "a node with a left subtree and a right subtree, each of which is itself a binary tree (or empty)" — so an algorithm that mirrors that definition falls out almost for free: handle the empty case directly, then combine whatever the left and right recursive calls return with the current node's value.

```python
def tree_sum(node):
    if node is None:
        return 0                      # base case
    return node.val + tree_sum(node.left) + tree_sum(node.right)  # recursive case
```

This pattern — null check, then combine two recursive results — is the skeleton underneath height computation, node counting, traversal, and most of the harder problems later in this group. Once it's second nature, most new tree problems are really just "what do I combine, and how" on top of an unchanged skeleton.

slides.subTitle: The shape guarantees interviewers actually test
slides.markdown:
A common vocabulary mix-up: assuming "balanced" means the same thing as "complete" or "full." It doesn't. **Balanced** (in the height-balance sense used by AVL trees and most interview problems) means: for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most some small constant (usually 1). A tree can be balanced without being complete — nodes don't need to fill left-to-right, they just can't lean too heavily to one side.

This distinction matters because "is this tree balanced" (checking height differences recursively) and "is this tree complete" (checking level-by-level fill order) are different algorithms answering different questions — conflating them leads to solving the wrong problem when a prompt says one term and you implement a check for the other.

slides.sectionTitle: Height, node count, and leaf count in one pass
slides.markdown:
All three metrics fall out of the same post-order-style recursion, computed together to avoid three separate O(n) passes:

```python
def stats(node):
    if node is None:
        return -1, 0, 0  # height, node_count, leaf_count
    lh, lc, ll = stats(node.left)
    rh, rc, rl = stats(node.right)
    height = 1 + max(lh, rh)
    count = 1 + lc + rc
    leaves = (ll + rl) if (node.left or node.right) else 1
    return height, count, leaves
```

Note the base case returns height `-1` for an empty subtree (so a single-node tree correctly computes height 0) — this is the height-as-edges convention; some codebases use height-as-nodes instead, which shifts every formula by one. Pick one convention and be consistent, and state which you're using if it's ambiguous from context.

slides.subTitle: The off-by-one that breaks base-case comparisons

slides.sectionTitle: Vocabulary as a foundation, not trivia
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to treat height/depth/balanced/complete as interview vocabulary to memorize and move past quickly. In practice, precision here prevents real bugs: a solution to "check if a tree is balanced" that secretly checks completeness, or a height function whose convention silently disagrees with a caller's assumption, produces wrong answers that are hard to spot in review because the code runs without error — it just answers a subtly different question than the one asked.

Every later topic in this group — traversals, BSTs, LCA, self-balancing trees — leans on getting height, depth, and the shape vocabulary exactly right, so it's worth the extra care here rather than treating it as throat-clearing before the "real" algorithm.
